name: William Congreve
credit: William Congreve, by Sir Godfrey Kneller, 1709 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Congreve (1670–1729) was the leading comic dramatist of the English Restoration stage, author of Love for Love (1695) and The Way of the World (1700). He also wrote songs, odes and translations, and was admired by Dryden and Pope.

The 4 poems here are the pieces printed under his name in Frederick Locker's Lyra Elegantiarum (London: E. Moxon, 1867), an anthology of vers de société and vers d'occasion by deceased authors; the texts follow that first edition.

poems.title: Tell me no more I am deceived
poems.author: William Congreve
poems.collection: Lyra Elegantiarum, ed. Frederick Locker (London: E. Moxon, 1867)
poems.text:
Tell me no more I am deceived,
That Chloe's false and common;
I always knew (at least believed)
She was a very woman:
As such I liked, as such caress'd,
She still was constant when possess'd,
She could do more for no man.

But O! her thoughts on others ran;
And that you think a hard thing!
Perhaps she fancied you the man;
And what care I one farthing?
You think she's false, I'm sure she's kind,
I take her face, and you her mind,
Who has the better bargain?

poems.title: Fair Amoret is gone astray
poems.author: William Congreve
poems.collection: Lyra Elegantiarum, ed. Frederick Locker (London: E. Moxon, 1867)
poems.text:
Fair Amoret is gone astray.
Pursue, and seek her, every lover;
I'll tell the signs by which you may
The wandering shepherdess discover.

Coquet and coy at once her air.
Both studied, tho' both seem neglected;
Careless she is, with artful care.
Affecting to seem unaffected.

With skill her eyes dart every glance.
Yet change so soon you'd ne'er suspect them;
For she'd persuade they wound by chance,
Though certain aim and art direct them.

She likes herself, yet others hates
For that which in herself she prizes;
And, while she laughs at them, forgets
She is the thing that she despises.

poems.title: False tho' she be to me and love
poems.author: William Congreve
poems.collection: Lyra Elegantiarum, ed. Frederick Locker (London: E. Moxon, 1867)
poems.text:
False tho' she be to me and love,
I'll ne'er pursue revenge;
For still the charmer I approve,
Tho' I deplore her change.
In hours of bliss we oft have met,
They could not always last;
And tho' the present I regret,
I'm grateful for the past.

poems.title: Pious Selinda goes to prayers
poems.author: William Congreve
poems.collection: Lyra Elegantiarum, ed. Frederick Locker (London: E. Moxon, 1867)
poems.text:
Pious Selinda goes to prayers,
If I but ask her favour;
And yet the silly fool's in tears,
If she believes I'll leave her.

Would I were free from this restraint,
Or else had hopes to win her:
Would she could make of me a saint,
Or I of her a sinner.

poems.title: See, see, she wakes! Sabina wakes
poems.author: William Congreve
poems.collection: The Home Book of Verse, ed. B. E. Stevenson (1912)

poems.title: Silly Fair
poems.author: William Congreve
poems.collection: The New Library of Poetry and Song, ed. W. C. Bryant (1876)
poems.text:
When Lesbia first I saw so heavenly fair,
With eyes so bright, and with that awful air,
I thought my heart which durst so high aspire
As bold as his who snatched celestial fire.
But soon as e'er the beauteous idiot spoke
Forth from her coral lips such nonsense broke,
Like balm the trickling nonsense healed my wound,
And what her eyes enthralled her tongue unbound.
